subject: fix(updates): decode add-spec and add-sort-order unbound (#1873)
body:
* fix(updates): decode add-spec and add-sort-order unbound

A commit request's add-spec and add-sort-order payloads are bound to a
schema by Apply, not by the decoder: AddPartitionSpec calls BindToSchema
and AddSortOrder calls CheckCompatibility, both against the table's
current schema. Decoding them into the bound types therefore enforced an
invariant the wire form does not carry.

That rejected a spec a client is entitled to send. A dropped partition
field is a void transform over source ID 0, which BindToSchema preserves
as a tombstone, so re-sending a spec after dropping a partition column
failed with "partition source ID must be positive: 0" before binding ran.

Decode into UnboundPartitionSpec and UnboundSortOrder, and hand the
embedded bound values to the builder. Source IDs that do not resolve are
still rejected, now by binding, which reports them against the schema
that decides. The constructors keep taking bound values, so callers are
unaffected, and Apply reports a nil payload rather than dereferencing it.

* fix(updates): exercise the add-spec and add-sort-order assertions

TestUnmarshalUpdates cast both sides of every comparison from the decoded
slice, so each update was compared against itself and the add-spec and
add-sort-order assertions passed vacuously. The add-spec branch was also
labelled "add-partition-spec", which no action matches, so it fell
through to the default branch and never ran at all.

Iterate over the expected updates, switch on the action constants, and
compare the expected value against the decoded one. The sort order
fixture disagreed with its JSON on the null order of the second field,
which the self-comparison hid; the JSON is the source of truth, so the
fixture now says nulls-last.

Assert the binding error the unresolvable source ID test expects, rather
than only the absence of the old decode error, and align the nil payload
guards with the "update %q requires field %q" template that
validateRequiredUpdateFields uses, so both paths read alike.

The addSortOrderUpdate comment claimed a parity with the partition spec
that does not hold. CheckCompatibility still requires every sort source
ID to resolve against the current schema, so decoding unbound defers the
error rather than accepting the field; say that instead.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Pütz <tobias@minio.io>

* docs(partitions,sort): cover the commit path in the unbound types

The unbound spec and sort order types documented themselves as the
create-table request's decode target and told readers to use the bound
types for anything read from table metadata. An add-spec or
add-sort-order commit payload is neither: its source IDs are the current
schema's field IDs, but nothing resolves them until the update is
applied, so decoding it bound enforces an invariant the wire form does
not carry. The types were already right for that payload; only their
docs excluded it.

Describe both wire forms, keep the create-table binding caveat scoped to
the form it applies to, and say that decoding unbound defers the check
rather than dropping it. Note as well that a bound spec's source IDs are
positive apart from the void tombstone a dropped field leaves behind,
which is the one case the bound decoder already lets through.

Also address the review's smaller points: comment that the builder
aliases the update's embedded sort order, because AddSortOrder writes the
fresh order ID into it and keeps a pointer to that field; use
require.ErrorContains where a test pins BindToSchema's wording, so a
regression stops with a useful message; and add the missing happy-path
round trip for the add-sort-order decode, which until now was only
covered on the reject path.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Pütz <tobias@minio.io>

* review comments

subject: fix(catalog/sql): return ErrNamespaceAlreadyExists on a concurrent create (#1635)
body:
* fix(catalog/sql): return ErrNamespaceAlreadyExists on a concurrent create

CreateNamespace resolves the namespace key, returns ErrNamespaceAlreadyExists if
it is there, and otherwise inserts. Two callers creating the same namespace both
pass that check, and the loser's insert then violates the primary key on
iceberg_namespace_properties. The driver's error is returned as-is:

  error inserting namespace properties for namespace '[raw]': constraint failed:
  UNIQUE constraint failed: iceberg_namespace_properties.catalog_name, ...

so callers matching errors.Is(err, catalog.ErrNamespaceAlreadyExists) -- the
contract every other catalog implementation honours -- see a create-if-absent
fail for a namespace that does exist.

Re-resolve the key when the insert fails and return the sentinel if the
namespace is now present. An insert that failed for any other reason is
unchanged.

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

* test(catalog/sql): pin the insert-recovery branch

TestCreateNamespaceConcurrent cannot tell the two paths apart: the check at
1246 and the recovery at 1276 return the same sentinel with the same
formatting, so the counts hold whichever one a goroutine took.

Adds a test that only passes if the insert ran and failed. A driver wrapper
plants the row on the same connection just before the catalog's insert, as its
own statement -- sqlite rolls back the failing statement's own changes,
including anything a trigger did, so the plant has to be separate.

The re-check now runs in the transaction. On a separate connection it could not
see an uncommitted winner, and with a constrained pool it deadlocked waiting
for a connection the open transaction was holding.

Also collects unexpected errors in the concurrent test and asserts after the
drain, so one stray error does not report as three failures.

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

* fix(catalog/sql): recover the create race with a savepoint

The insert-failure recovery re-queried the namespace on the same tx. On
Postgres a failed statement aborts the whole transaction (25P02), so that
re-check came back an error rather than a row and the raw duplicate-key
error was returned -- the pre-PR behaviour. The fix was inert on Postgres,
one of the five declared dialects, and SQLite masked it by rolling back
only the failing statement.

Wrap the insert in a savepoint (bun's nested transaction, which emits the
right syntax per dialect, including MSSQL's SAVE TRANSACTION). On failure,
roll back to the savepoint so the transaction is usable again, then
re-check. The race-loser now returns the sentinel in the same form as the
serial pre-check so the two paths are identical; the rollback- and
re-check-failure branches join their causes instead of dropping them.

TestCreateNamespaceLosesInsertRace drives a driver that emulates the
Postgres abort -- refusing statements after the failed insert until a
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT -- so it fails without the savepoint and passes with
it, which the previous SQLite-only planting driver could not show. Adds a
negative test that an unrelated insert failure surfaces its own error, and
a note that the driver name depends on databaseName() being unique.

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

* fix(catalog/sql): gate the create-race savepoint to Postgres

Oracle has no RELEASE SAVEPOINT, so sp.Commit() on the happy path would
fail and roll back a good insert. Only Postgres aborts the whole tx on a
failed statement, so only it needs the savepoint to keep the re-check
runnable; other dialects take a plain insert + re-check.

The emulated-Postgres recovery tests now build the catalog with the
Postgres dialect and assert the insert interceptor actually fired.

* test(catalog/sql): pin non-Postgres recovery and savepoint happy path

Add a deterministic SQLite-dialect test (non-aborting dupInsertDriver) for
the non-Postgres recovery branch, and an insertSucceeds mode covering the
Postgres SAVEPOINT -> insert -> RELEASE happy path. Both previously ran at
coverage count 0. Also scope the gate comment to the dialects reasoned about.

* test(catalog/sql): assert the savepoint happy path persists the row

The success-path test only checked the nil return, so swapping RELEASE
SAVEPOINT for ROLLBACK left it green while zero rows persisted. Let the
insertSucceeds probe read real persistence and assert the namespace
survives the commit, so a rolled-back savepoint fails the test.

---------

subject: feat(table): add explicit default spec/sort-order commit fence (Transaction.AssertDefaultShape) (#1891)
body:
feat(table): add Transaction.AssertDefaultShape (Java UpdateRequirements parity)

Java UpdateRequirements.forUpdateTable registers AssertDefaultSpecID
and AssertDefaultSortOrderID when a commit changes those defaults, but
commits that stage no spec or sort-order change of their own (for
example a properties-only revision marker) carry no shape assertion, so
two racers evolving a table's declaration can interleave. AssertDefaultShape
is the explicit fence — the shape analogue of AssertRefSnapshotID —
pinning both defaults at their base values. Requirements deduplicate
against the producer-built assertions UpdateSpec and ReplaceSortOrder
already register.

subject: fix(table): drain RollingDataWriter's recordCh on mid-stream write errors (#1851)
body:
* fix(table): drain RollingDataWriter's recordCh on mid-stream write errors

When stream() exits early on a write error, it deregisters itself from
writerFactory.writers before abortAll() can run, so batches already
queued in recordCh were never released.

A lockless drain is not enough: an Add that has passed its closed check
can still enqueue after the drain sees the channel empty, stranding a
retained record. Add and stream's shutdown now share an RWMutex barrier.
Add holds the read lock across its check-and-enqueue; stream's cleanup
cancels the context (releasing any parked send), takes the write lock
(which blocks until every active Add has returned), sets noMoreSends so
later Add calls bail before retaining, then drains. recordCh is never
closed from stream, so a live sender can't hit a closed channel.

Fixes #1825.

Signed-off-by: deepak-2605 <108828387+deepak-2605@users.noreply.github.com>

* fix(table): address review — guard cleanup cancel, fix test goroutine leaks

Review follow-up for #1851:

- Only cancel ctx from stream's cleanup on the error exit. The clean
  exit reaches cleanup after closeInput already closed the input with
  all senders finished, so there are no parked sends to release and
  cancelling there only signalled a failure that did not happen. Gated
  behind an exitedCleanly flag.
- Reword the "recordCh is never closed here" comment: another goroutine
  may close it via closeInput, and the drain's !ok case is what ends the
  loop then — it is not dead code.
- Pair both new tests' manually built writers with defer factory.closeAll()
  (stops the iter.Pull counter goroutine) and defer cancel() (the context
  otherwise leaks if the test bails before stream starts).

subject: test(table): fix TruncateUpperBoundBinary guard for negative width (#1980)
body:
The negative-width test case ("negative width keeps bound") was added in
#1934 while the stricter truncation-invariant guard was added in #1928.
Each PR was green on its own base, but the rebase-merge combined them:
the guard `tt.truncate < len(tt.value)` matches a negative width (-1 < 2),
so the negative case (where the bound is kept, not truncated) wrongly
falls into the truncation asserts and fails deterministically:

    utils_test.go:128: "2" is not less than or equal to "-1"
    utils_test.go:129: "0" is not greater than "0"

Only assert the shrink/increment invariants when a truncation actually
happened by additionally requiring a non-negative width. The production
TruncateUpperBoundBinary already handles negative widths correctly.
